content.p: On the evening of Tuesday 13 November 1990, a 33-year-old unemployed man named David Gray began shooting his neighbours in Aramoana, a tiny settlement at the entrance to Otago Harbour. By the time police shot him dead about a day later, he had killed 13 people, according to New Zealand Police. The dead included a police sergeant and four children. It was the worst criminal massacre New Zealand had known, as the Otago Daily Times put it at the time, and it remained the country's deadliest mass shooting for 29 years, until the Christchurch mosque attacks of 2019.

Because Gray died at the scene, no trial was held and no court has tested what happened. What is known comes from police statements, newspaper reporting from 1990 and later, and the recollections of people who were there.
content.h2: A village at the end of the road
content.p: Aramoana lies 27 kilometres from Dunedin. The Otago Daily Times reported in 1990 that it normally had 40 to 50 residents, mostly retired people, alongside several families living alternative lifestyles. The country around it included sand dunes, tussock grassland and salt marsh.

Gray lived at 27 Muri Street. The Otago Daily Times described him as a loner who had caused concern among residents and others in Dunedin with his fascination for guns and the military. Action on Armed Violence, a charity that studies gun violence, records that he was a licensed gun owner. He had been issued a new licence in 1984 after what it called "limited vetting", because he already owned a bolt-action rifle. By November 1990 he owned six rifles, four of them semi-automatic, and the law of the time set no limit on how much ammunition he could hold.

A Dunedin gun shop assistant, Howard Halliday, later told the Otago Daily Times that Gray had bought a Norinco rifle, a copy of the AK-47 pattern, and a .22 rifle from the shop almost a year before the killings. A few days before the shootings, Halliday said, Gray had come in for ammunition and mentioned shooting a seagull on the beach. Halliday said he found that odd, and phoned police when he heard of the shooting. He told the newspaper that Gray had behaved inappropriately on several occasions without it ever reaching police.

The Otago Daily Times reported that Gray began firing with automatic and semi-automatic weapons shortly after 7.30 pm. The paper noted that why he did so was not known. Some locals suggested a grudge against his next-door neighbour, Garry Holden, who had Tapanui flu, a chronic illness also called ME. According to those locals, Gray claimed Holden had passed the virus on to him. This was a rumour reported at the time, not an established motive.

The Otago Daily Times and Action on Armed Violence agree on the opening of the attack. Gray shot Holden, then set the Holden house on fire. Later reporting by the same newspaper says Holden, 38, was struck seven times, an attack witnessed by his two young daughters, Chiquita and Jasmine, and by Rewa Bryson, the daughter of his partner Julie-Anne. Gray found Chiquita and shot her in the arm; the bullet entered her chest and abdomen. She survived by escaping through a back door and running past her father's body. Because the house was burned, the coroner could not determine how the other girls died. Rewa's age is given as 11 by 1News and as 9 by the Otago Daily Times.

Gray then fired on people in the street and on passing vehicles. Action on Armed Violence records that he killed two six-year-old boys and wounded a four-year-old girl, and that he entered a house and killed people inside. The Otago Daily Times named the child hurt as Stacey Percy, 4, of Careys Bay, and listed Vanessa Grace Percy, 26, among the dead. The newspaper's later reporting identified one of the six-year-olds as Leo Wilson, who died of shock from his gunshot wounds. John Banks, the police minister, visited Aramoana the next morning and recalled the fear on the boy's face.
The newspaper said in 1990 that those believed to be among the victims included Vic Crimp, a former mayor of Green Island, and Garry Holden, a leader of the campaign against an aluminium smelter.

Sergeant Stewart Guthrie, 41, the sole charge officer at Port Chalmers police station, responded immediately, according to New Zealand Police, which says he knew the gunman. The Otago Daily Times reported that residents had called him to the village. According to the police account, Guthrie and Constable Russell Anderson found Gray at his home and began containing him. When Gray retreated to the rear of the property, Guthrie challenged him. Gray fired a series of shots, one of which killed the sergeant.

The Otago Daily Times of 14 November described the sergeant as missing and feared dead. The paper reported that bodies stayed in the streets overnight; officers dared not go near them while the gunman was armed and at large. Residents were still trapped in their homes that morning; others had been taken out to Port Chalmers.

The paper said squads of armed police from four southern cities, Dunedin, Christchurch, Timaru and Invercargill, were rushed in. It reported that, early on 14 November, police believed the gunman was somewhere between Te Ngaru and Spit Beach and decided to wait for first light. Gray was wearing commando gear and had blacked his face, the Otago Daily Times said, and according to Action on Armed Violence he fired at a police helicopter and at officers during the standoff.

Soon after midday, according to the Otago Daily Times, a helicopter landed at Heyward Point and two anti-terrorist police officers from Wellington climbed down towards the township. Officers worked through the houses. Shortly after 4 pm police advanced on Gray's house in Muri Street with smoke grenades and tear gas. Just before 6 pm there were short bursts of about 50 rounds. Police said the squads approached the corner of Mokia and Poto streets and were met with a volley of shots. Gray was shot by anti-terrorist squad members. The paper reported that police first said he had been arrested with serious head and chest injuries, and that he was pronounced dead at 6.20 pm at the scene.

Tim Ashton, a member of the anti-terrorist squad sent to Aramoana, later told RNZ about the operation. Early reports of the toll changed as police released names. The Otago Daily Times said on 15 November that at least 11 had died with two unaccounted for, and its list of names brought the toll to 14, counting Gray.

Sources do not all give the same number. New Zealand Police and 1News say Gray killed 13 people. Action on Armed Violence lists 12 killed by gunshot, counting the gunman, and two in the arson attack. The Otago Daily Times in 1990 put the toll at 14 including Gray. The pages do not explain how these counts relate to one another.

Guthrie was posthumously awarded the George Cross for conspicuous gallantry. In 2018 the Otago Daily Times reported that his three grown-up children had sold the medal privately to Lord Michael Ashcroft, a British peer and collector of gallantry medals. The Herald on Sunday had been told that their mother, Sandra, wanted it sold before she died the previous October, because she had always worried about its security. The Ministry for Culture and Heritage approved its export under the Protected Objects Act 1975. Ashcroft said he would display it at the Imperial War Museum in London.

The Arms Act 1983 had introduced lifetime firearms licences for people over 16 judged "fit and proper". It required no registration of weapons, and a licence holder could own as many as he wished, Action on Armed Violence says. John Banks had been police minister for only weeks when the shootings took place. He later told the Otago Daily Times that he led the push for reform but had to bring forward a watered-down bill because of resistance from rural members of his own National Party caucus.

The Arms Amendment Act 1992 required a special endorsement and acquisition permit for military-style semi-automatic weapons, according to Action on Armed Violence. It ended lifetime licences in favour of ten-year ones, required a licence to buy ammunition, restricted mail-order purchases and tightened storage rules. The Otago Daily Times adds that photographs became necessary for new licences. A full ban on such weapons was rejected, the charity says, because compensating owners would have cost too much and gun-rights groups opposed it. Labour, then in opposition, had proposed a ban.

A 1997 review by Sir Thomas Thorp concluded that, because compliance was low, the 1992 changes were not effective and radical reform was needed. A bill based on a 1996 government-ordered review failed in 1999 after strong opposition in Parliament. Ashton, who was among those campaigning for tougher controls, called the aftermath a "missed opportunity". After the Christchurch attacks in 2019, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern announced a ban on military-style semi-automatics and assault rifles five days afterwards. The Otago Daily Times reported that a second round of reform, passed in 2020, paved the way for a register.

A memorial stands in the dunes beyond the township, with the names of the dead on one side, according to RNZ. On 14 November 2020, the thirtieth anniversary, relatives, police officers, paramedics and members of the Armed Offenders Squad gathered there, in what 1News called one of the largest organised gatherings since the tragedy. The 13 names were read aloud. Julie-Anne Tamati, who was shot at and survived, had lost her fiance Garry and her daughter Rewa. "Sometimes I think, 30 years, I should be over it, but you just don't get over it," she told 1News. She told the Otago Daily Times she had felt support for survivors was lacking at the time.

Police Commissioner Andrew Coster said on the anniversary that the grief of those who knew the dead was felt as keenly as it was then. Sergeant Guthrie's nephew, Superintendent Jason Guthrie, said he had always admired his uncle's police work.
